intuition: For n input positions, the smallest missing positive number must be between 1 and n + 1. Use the array itself to remember which of these numbers exist. Place value 1 at index 0, value 2 at index 1, and so on. Then look for the first position with the wrong value.

Give each relevant value x a home at index x-1. If the current value belongs somewhere else, swap it into that home and inspect the new value that arrived. Repeating this operation is essential because a single index may expose an entire chain of misplaced values. Out-of-range values carry no useful membership information.

A duplicate needs special care: if its home already contains the same value, swapping makes no progress and would loop forever. Otherwise every swap establishes one correct home permanently. A final scan asks whether position i contains i+1; its first failure is the missing positive. If every home is filled, n+1 is the answer.

A swap cannot displace a correct home: if destination x-1 already contained x, the duplicate guard would prevent that swap. Therefore every executed swap permanently fills one new correct home, even if its displaced value starts another chain.

steps: For nums=[3,4,-1,1], n=4, so only values 1 through 4 need homes.
At i=0, value 3 has home=3-1=2. Swap indices 0 and 2 to get [-1,4,3,1]; -1 is out of range and stops this chain.
At i=1, value 4 has home=3. Swap indices 1 and 3 to get [-1,1,3,4]. Now value 1 has home=0; swapping indices 1 and 0 gives [1,-1,3,4].
The placement phase ends with [1,-1,3,4]. Three and four are already in their correct homes.
The scan accepts index 0 because it contains 1, then fails at index 1. Return 2.

codeNotes.code: while 1 <= nums[i] <= n and nums[nums[i] - 1] != nums[i]:
codeNotes.note: The range check prevents invalid indexing, while the inequality prevents duplicate-value cycles.
Swapping fills a home without losing the displaced value; the surrounding while loop processes that newly exposed value.
After placement, membership is encoded positionally. The first mismatched slot identifies the smallest absent positive, not merely any missing number.

keyDecision: Swap only a value in 1..n whose destination does not already contain that value.

concept.question: Could each small positive number mark its own parking space?
intuition: Sorting or keeping a separate membership collection would solve the problem but uses additional work or memory. With four input positions, a missing positive must be among 1 through 5; huge and negative values cannot be the smallest missing one.

Give each relevant value a home: 1 belongs in the first position, 2 in the second, and so on. Move a value into its home by exchanging it with what is there. Then the first home lacking its proper resident reveals the missing positive.
concept.observation: Move only values within the available home range, and stop if their home already contains the same value.
approach: Place each value from one through the input length in its matching position.
Ignore negatives, zero, oversized values, and already placed duplicates.
Scan for the first missing resident; if every home is full, return one beyond the last home.
concept.correctness: The answer is at most one more than the number of input positions: if all smaller positives are present, that next number is missing. Each successful exchange fills a value’s designated home and never needs to dislodge a correctly placed different value. After placement, a positive is present exactly when its home contains it, so the first failed home test gives the smallest missing positive.

complexity.explanation: Although one position may trigger several exchanges, every successful exchange places another relevant value. There are only linearly many placements and one final scan. The original row supplies the memory, so auxiliary memory is constant.

pitfalls: Stop on a duplicate already in its home.
Return one beyond the length if all homes are filled.
